newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge keeps accused South Korean spy in jail.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge keeps accused South Korean spy in jail.

text.p: U.S. Navy computer specialist Robert Kim, accused of passing dozens of secret documents to South Korea, must remain in jail until his trial on espionage charges, a federal judge ruled on Wednesday.
U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema granted a request by federal government prosecutors and overturned a magistrate's earlier ruling that Kim should be freed on a $200,000 bond while he awaits trial.

"At this point, the evidence appears overwhelming," the judge said from the bench, adding that the likelihood of conviction was "quite high," increasing the risk that Kim might try to flee the country.

The Korean-born Kim, 56, an 18-year government employee who became a U.S. citizen in 1974, has been accused of passing more than 40 confidential or secret documents to a South Korean Embassy official since May. He was arrested last week while attending a diplomatic reception.

Prosecutor Robert Chesnut said U.S. investigators secretly videotaped Kim meeting with South Korean officials in March at a Washington-area hotel to discuss the possibility that he might work for Seoul after retiring from U.S. Navy intelligence.
"I myself am a Korean, and I want to help the Korean government," Chesnut quoted Kim as saying at the meeting.
The prosecutor told a court hearing Kim wanted to work as a consultant for South Korea on computers and intelligence matters.

Brinkema said a transcript of the meeting suggests Kim was trying to exploit his current job "to curry favour with South Korean officials" and was "looking very seriously at a post-retirement business connection with the South Korean government."

In ordering that Kim stay in jail, she cited the serious nature of his alleged crime, saying unauthorised disclosures of classified information "undermine the integrity of the security system of American intelligence."
Although Kim has no prior criminal record, the judge said he has strong ties to South Korea and faces a likely sentence of seven to nine years in prison on the charges he now faces.
Chesnut said prosecutors planned to seek a grand jury indictment charging Kim with violating the espionage law, a crime that carries a maximum penalty of life in prison.
Four families who know Kim from their church have offered to put up the equity in their homes to secure his release on bond, but the judge said, "I am not satisifed that would be enough."
Defence attorney James Clark argued for Kim's release, saying he had engaged in an "ill-advised effort to pass information to a friendly nation about its traditional adversaries."
He said during the 50-minute hearing that prosecutors had failed to show that Kim intended to harm national security.
